title: What He left unsaid
hookLine: Allah set duties and limits, and kept silent on things out of mercy, not forgetfulness, so don't dig into them
tomorrow: want to be loved? tomorrow's hadith says: want less. wait, what?

cards: Some rulebooks try to cover everything. Every case spelled out, and somehow each new rule breeds two more questions. Yesterday ended on a puzzle: how can leaving something unsaid be mercy?
Hadith thirty, reported by Abu Tha'labah, has an odd phrase in it.
Allah has set duties, so don't neglect them; set limits, so don't cross them; forbidden things, so don't violate them; and kept silent about other things, out of mercy for you, not out of forgetting.
Not out of forgetting. Why would anyone need to be told that?

teach.h: A SILENCE LOOKS LIKE A GAP.
teach.b: Because a careful mind treats every silence as a gap. If the text didn't mention it, surely someone missed something, so let's dig until we find a rule.
The hadith closes that door: the silence is on purpose, and it's a gift. That's the solve. The open space is part of the plan.
Then the last line: so don't go digging into them. Sahih Muslim has a scene that shows why. The Prophet, peace be upon him, tells the people that hajj, the pilgrimage, has been made a duty.
A man asks: every year? The Prophet stays silent.
The man asks again, and again, three times. Then the Prophet says, in paraphrase: if I had said yes, it would have become a duty, and you couldn't have done it. Leave me be as long as I leave you be.
The Qur'an says it too, in Pickthall's words: "Ask not of things which, if they were made known unto you, would trouble you."
Jurists drew a principle from texts like these: in ordinary things, the starting point is that they're allowed.
Here's something to tell a friend tonight: the silence isn't a hole in the law. It's room to live in, left there on purpose.

how: Muslim jurists distinguish what the texts require, what they forbid, and what they leave open; in everyday matters, the common starting point is that a thing is allowed unless a text says otherwise.

games.q: what does “what he left unsaid” mean?
o: secrets the Prophet told only a few friends
rules hidden in the Qur'an for experts
the things Allah left open, as a mercy

p: asked three times; he stayed silent

s: the hadith says some things went unmentioned because they were forgotten
the opposite: out of mercy for you, not out of forgetting.
a careful believer should hunt down a rule for every detail
the hadith ends: so don't go digging into them.
when a man kept asking if hajj was every year, the Prophet stayed silent at first
then he said: if I had said yes, it would have become a duty.

games.q: a friend just started praying and is stressed, hunting for a rule on every tiny detail no text mentions. what does hadith thirty offer?
o: keep the clear duties and limits; where the texts are silent, that's room.
find a rule for every detail first; nothing should be left open.
if some things are open, then the duties are optional too.
games.why: the hadith keeps the duties and limits firm, and calls the silence a mercy: don't dig into it.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write by hand one question you keep circling, the one you've asked yourself five different ways. Underneath it, write: this one can rest.
For the sit, keep your hand flat on the paper and let the question stay open, unanswered, without poking at it.

wordCard.voice: What He left unsaid: the things Allah kept silent about, not forgotten, but left open as a mercy, so nobody has to dig them up.

orig.note: Arabic: He was silent about things, as a mercy for you. the heart of hadith thirty.

carryVoice: For the road: silence is mercy too, and open space can be a gift. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in al-Nawawiyyah, hadith 30 (Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani; from al-Daraqutni)
Sahih Muslim 1337 (hajj: 'every year?'; leave me as long as I leave you)

sources.q: Ask not of things which, if they were made known unto you, would trouble you
